document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
) 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms 
) 
) 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
 
 
 
POST-CONFERENCE STATEMENT OF  
CONSTELLATION ENERGY GENERATION, LLC 
 
Pursuant to the Commission’s July 30, 2026 notice in the above-captioned proceeding,1 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (Constellation) submits these comments addressing issues 
raised at the Commissioner-led technical conference held on July 23, 2026, and responding to the 
Commission’s issues list found in the appendix of the Notice.    
I. 
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY   
Constellation commends the Commission for proactively addressing issues with the PJM 
stakeholder process.  While we caution against overhauling a governance process that, despite its 
challenges, has led to the successful implementation of many market enhancements over the years, 
resulting in a regional market that saves consumers approximately $5 billion annually,2 there are 
nonetheless a number of reforms that can be made to improve the efficiency of the existing 
stakeholder process.  As explained in responses to the Commission’s questions, Constellation does 
not support altering section 205 filing right authority or reforms that may result in undue political 
influence on market rules.  Most of the unrest in PJM over the last decade has involved issues 
related to resource adequacy, generator retirements and replacements, and capacity market rules 
changes—matters over which PJM already has section 205 filing rights and is able to take action 
 
1 PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms, Notice Requesting Post-Conference Comment, Docket No. AD26-7-
000 (July 30, 2026) (Notice).  
2 The Value of PJM, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (Jan. 21, 2026), https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/about-
pjm/the-value-of-pjm.pdf.

2 
 
under section 205 even when the Membership disagrees.  Instead, Constellation urges the 
Commission to focus on reforms that are tailored to the problems the region is trying to solve, 
including the suggestions we offer herein (with a more detailed path forward in the appendix).   
II. 
QUESTION RESPONSES 
A. PJM Board Independence 
1. Should Board members’ terms be extended to five or more years? 
 
Yes.  Board terms should be lengthened to five years with two full terms possible, and 
substantive criteria should be considered for removing Board members.  Terms exceeding five 
years may be too long of a commitment period for Board member candidates and could 
inadvertently limit Board member candidates.  Further discussion on this matter should be pursued. 
2. Should there be a maximum number of years that a Board member may serve (e.g., 10 
years)? 
 
Yes.  See our response to Question 1.  Constellation generally agrees that a maximum number 
of years is reasonable and welcomes discussion on determining the most appropriate number of 
years any Board member may serve.  For example, a limit of two, five-year terms—for a ten-year 
cap—could make sense.3   
3. Should the Board member qualification rules be revised to provide a preference for some 
Board members that reside in the PJM region?  
Yes.  The key focus on Board qualifications should remain (as it has in the past) on relevant 
experience and expertise.  If strictly applied, a residency requirement risks diminishing the number 
of otherwise qualified Board candidates.  Nonetheless, the deeper appreciation of a region that 
could be gained through living there (and being directly impacted by decisions made by the Board) 
could be beneficial.  Constellation recommends a requirement that one PJM Board member reside 
 
3 We would suggest not counting years served replacing a Board member who is leaving the Board prior to the end 
of her/his term against the ten-year cap.

3 
 
within the PJM footprint.  Having a one-member residency requirement is consistent with other 
Board membership qualification quantities in Section 7.2 of the Operating Agreement that can be 
satisfied with one qualified member (e.g., “one [member] shall have expertise and experience in 
the operation or concerns of transmission dependent utilities, one [member] shall have expertise 
and experience in the operation or planning of transmission systems, and one [member] shall have 
expertise and experience in the area of commercial markets and trading and associated risk 
management”).4 
4. Should the conflict-of-interest rules be revised to reduce the cooling off period for Board 
members from two years to one year? 
 
Yes.  The two-year cooling off period may unduly limit the pool of candidates—who are 
otherwise qualified—from Board participation.  A one-year cooling off period may be more 
appropriate and would be generally consistent with the Commission’s own cooling off period for 
former Commissioners and senior Commission staff.5  
5. Should restrictions on Board communications be relaxed to enable more communication 
between the Board and stakeholders? 
 
Yes.  Additional opportunities for Board and stakeholder communications should be pursued 
as long as such additional communication opportunities are fair for all stakeholders and Board 
independence is preserved.  
6. In order to increase transparency, should Board votes be made public or the Board be 
required to explain its reasoning?  
Yes.  While disclosing individual Board member votes would chill robust Board discussion of 
issues and should remain non-public, the Board should be required to provide a written explanation 
supporting its decisions and how the decision will achieve a just, reasonable and not unduly 
 
4 Operating Agreement, Section 7.2 (emphasis added). 
5 See 18 U.S.C. § 207(c); 5 C.F.R. § 2641.204.

4 
 
discriminatory or preferential outcome.  In addition, such explanation should include a discussion 
of why it rejected other views. 
7. In order to increase transparency, should some Board meetings be open or available to 
the public? 
No.  The PJM Board is a decision-making body, unlike the boards of some other RTOs/ISOs 
that advise on decisions being made by the RTO/ISO leadership.  The PJM Board therefore needs 
an independent opportunity to deliberate, and requiring all deliberation to occur in a public arena 
would chill effective Board meeting discussions.  Non-public Board meetings are necessary for 
efficient discussion of often very technical matters to support well-informed policy decisions.  To 
the extent additional information on Board decisions is desired, this can be addressed through a 
Board memo as described in our response to Question 6.  Additionally, the Board should consider 
making all relevant, non-confidential material presented by PJM staff, the market monitor, and 
other participants at Board meetings public contemporaneously with the meeting.  If additional 
Board interaction with stakeholders is pursued, as suggested in our response to Question 5, it must 
be fair for all stakeholders, preserve Board independence, and should be in addition to the existing, 
separate Board meetings.   
8. Should PJM’s governing documents be revised to explicitly state that the responsibility 
of PJM and its Board is to serve the public interest? 
No.  PJM is already required to provide service consistent with the public interest by Federal 
Power Act (FPA), 16 U.S.C. § 824d(a), and it would be redundant and encourage disputes to 
attempt to restate that obligation in PJM’s governing documents using different words.     
9. Should state representatives have at least one voting member on the Nominating 
Committee? 
No.  States can and should make their views known about selection of potential Board members 
by taking advantage of existing opportunities to engage.  This could include coordinating efforts

5 
 
by developing a list of suggested nominees, perhaps through OPSI or through the formation of 
nomination advisory group consisting of state-designated representatives.  Some suggest that the 
Board member selection is “slanted” and “deep[ly] biased” and seek to have specific interests 
dominate the Nominating Committee.6  Those suggestions are not correct.  A number of prior 
participants in the Nominating Committee, including two current Constellation employees, signed 
an affidavit being submitted contemporaneously in this proceeding explaining the robust and fair 
nature of the Nominating Committees’ work.   
10. Should PJM adopt public performance metrics and tie management compensation to 
their achievement? 
Yes.  To the extent the Board already has or adopts performance metrics for senior PJM 
management, those metrics should be made public. 
11. Should the stakeholder process be advisory, i.e., stakeholder votes only inform the 
Board? 
No.  The stakeholder process should not be made advisory-only and should remain as is for the 
reasons discussed below.7   
PJM’s Section 205 Filing Rights Should Remain As Is 
PJM has authority to file changes to rules related to resource adequacy issues under section 
205.  Section 205 filings related to energy and ancillary market matters (Operating Agreement, 
Schedule 1) and to regional transmission planning matters (Operating Agreement, Schedule 6) are 
conditioned on PJM first obtaining Members Committee approval, and PJM has complained that 
“PJM may be required to proceed under more restrictive requirements of section 206 [if it does 
 
6 See, e.g., Pre-Technical Conference Statement of Jacob Finkel, Office of Governor Josh Shapiro, Deputy Secretary 
of Policy, Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 9 (July 16, 2026). 
7 We interpret the suggestion of an “advisory” stakeholder process to mean that PJM would have filing rights under 
section 205 even if it would consider stakeholder input.

6 
 
not obtain Member Committee approval].”8  To avoid the “more restrictive” requirements of 
section 206, PJM seeks discretion to file under section 205 for energy and ancillary service market 
and regional transmission planning matters even if the PJM Members disagree.9  As discussed in 
the following sub-sections, PJM has no need for such authority, which could be more damaging 
than helpful.  Moreover, PJM lacks a legal basis to abrogate the long-standing allocation of section 
205 filing rights.10   
PJM’s Concern Is a Red-Herring and Is Unsupported 
Virtually all discussions of significance related to PJM in recent years focus on resource 
adequacy issues, where PJM already has section 205 authority.  For example, of the six principles 
involving PJM in the Statement of Principles Regarding PJM signed by the National Energy 
Dominance Counsel and all thirteen PJM state governors, PJM already has section 205 filing rights 
over all six principles.11  PJM’s concern (particularly with respect to filing authority over the 
energy and ancillary service markets) seem particularly out of place against this backdrop.  As 
Constellation’s Mason Emnett explained in a pre-conference statement filed in this proceeding:  
[M]ost of the unrest in PJM over the last decade has involved issues 
related 
to 
resource 
adequacy, 
generator 
retirements 
and 
replacements, and capacity market rules changes—matters over 
which PJM already has section 205 filing rights and is able to take 
action under section 205 even when the Membership disagrees. 
When PJM has delayed action, it has been because its leadership has 
decided not to proceed, not because of any lack of authority. In the 
 
8 Comments from PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 6 (July 16, 2026) (PJM Pre-Conference 
Comments). 
9 Id. at 6-7; see also FERC Mediation Term Sheet, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Term 1 (Aug. 10, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/committees/mc/2026/20260819/20260819-item-08---1-
ferc-mediation-term-sheet.pdf.  
10 As Constellation owns and operates generation assets, its focus in this discussion is on PJM authority over energy 
and ancillary services markets. 
11 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM, National Energy Dominance Council (Jan. 16, 2026), 
https://www.energy.gov/documents/statement-principles-regarding-pjm.  The seventh principle, regarding cost 
allocation, involves only the PJM state governors and not PJM.

7 
 
same vein, PJM’s lack of section 205 rights over energy market 
issues has not deterred PJM’s action under section 206 when its 
leadership decided to proceed without Membership endorsement.12 
There is no evidence contradicting Mr. Emnett’s statement, and PJM’s concerns are 
overstated and unsupported.  For example, in its pre-conference comments, PJM lists nine 
instances in recent years of a “failed” stakeholder vote.13  However, PJM’s recitation of recent 
stakeholder history deserves some scrutiny.  Of the nine “failed” stakeholder votes only one of the 
nine (i.e., 11%) did not involve a resource adequacy-related matter (over which PJM already has 
section 205 filing authority).14  In other words, the stakeholder vote is already advisory for eight 
of the items listed, so PJM could file under section 205 regardless of the voting outcome.  For the 
one item not covered under PJM’s section 205 rights, reserve requirement revisions, a majority 
(although not a required super-majority) of Members did support PJM’s proposal.  And a separate 
proposal on reserve deployment revisions was endorsed by acclamation.   
PJM raised a single instance where it believes the lack of unfettered section 205 filing 
rights has undermined its ability to make needed reform (i.e., certain reserves markets 
improvements).15  While Constellation fully supports reserve market improvements, we are 
concerned, based on PJM’s track record with respect to resource adequacy (described below), 
whether PJM would actually exercise its authority in a manner that alleviates, rather than 
contributes to, the “credibility gap” discussed in PJM’s recent paper.  With respect to the issue of 
reserve market reforms referenced by PJM, Constellation notes that PJM failed to vigorously 
pursue it in the designated senior task force, which contributed to its delay progressing through the 
 
12 Pre-Conference Statement of Mason Emnett on Behalf of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, Docket 
No. AD26-7-000, at 2 (July 16, 2026). 
13 PJM Pre-Conference Comments at 3-4. 
14 Id. at 4. 
15 Id.

8 
 
stakeholder process.  It is PJM’s failure to timely articulate the needs and goals of the reserve 
stakeholder process, rather than Member voting, that is responsible for delay of these much-needed 
reforms.  If PJM believes this reserves change is critical, then it should not have allowed the 
stakeholder process to languish as it did and PJM should not be allowed to point to this process—
where it contributed significantly to the delay—as justifying its claim for section 205 filing rights.   
In addition, rather than pursue complete abrogation of the Members’ long-standing section 
205 filing rights, PJM could pursue reform via other means.  Specifically, PJM can file a well-
supported proposal under section 206 of FPA.  Section 206 of the FPA is the long-established 
means for those lacking section 205 filing rights to seek recourse, and courts unsurprisingly agree 
that section 206 provides an adequate remedy.16  PJM arguments that section 206 is “more 
restrictive” compared to section 205 are not relevant under the FPA if there is no underlying right 
to file under section 205.  As the Commission found in a recent decision responding to a similar 
PJM complaint about section 206 filings, “the fact that PJM may benefit from what it views as a 
more timely and efficient process under FPA section 205 compared to section 206 does not render 
the [transmission planning] Protocol’s existing location in the OA to be unjust and 
unreasonable.”17  PJM has demonstrated skill at filing under section 206, particularly in response 
to an urgent situation,18 so it is unclear there is a problem at all.  Simply put, PJM has not 
demonstrated that there is any meaningful issue that it cannot already address. 
 
16 See, e.g., Sacramento Mun. Util. Dist. v. FERC, 616 F.3d 520, 542 (D.C. Cir. 2010) (in the event of “an unjust 
outcome, San Diego may petition the Commission to order appropriate changes . . .  under section 206”).  
17 Duquesne Light Co., 189 FERC ¶ 61,181, at P 106 (2024), order on reh’g, 192 FERC ¶ 61,051 (2025), aff’d sub 
nom. PJM Transmission Owners v. FERC, Nos. 25-1064, 25-1100, 2026 U.S. App. LEXIS 16255 (D.C. Cir. June 5, 
2026). 
18 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 178 FERC ¶ 61,104 (PJM filing to change transmission constraint penalty 
factor contained within the Operating Agreement so as to avoid unjust and unreasonable energy market rates for 
consumers on the Northern Neck peninsula in the Dominion Transmission Zone), order on reh’g, 179 FERC 
¶ 61,161 (2022), aff’d sub nom. Citadel FNGE Ltd. v. FERC, 77 F.4th 842 (D.C. Cir. 2023).

9 
 
The Members’ Retention of Section 205 Filing Rights Was Heavily Negotiated and Cannot Be 
Set Aside Because PJM Wants Control 
Nor can the Members Committee section 205 filing rights be abrogated simply because 
PJM wants control.  The allocation of those rights, as set forth in Sections 8.8 and 10.4 of the 
Operating Agreement, is entitled to Mobile-Sierra protection,19 meaning that by operation of law 
the filing rights can only be abrogated upon a finding of “unequivocal public necessity” or 
“extraordinary circumstances.”20   
Section 8.8 grants the Members Committee the authority to “amend any portion of this 
Agreement, including the Schedules hereto, or create new Schedules, and file any such 
amendments or new Schedules with FERC.”21  This includes Schedule 1, which governs the energy 
and ancillary services markets.  Section 10.4 sets forth PJM’s duties and responsibilities, including 
“[filing] on behalf of the Members any amendments to this Agreement or the Schedules hereto, 
any new Schedules hereto, and mak[ing] any other regulatory filings on behalf of the Members or 
the LLC necessary to implement this Agreement.”22  Thus, while the Members entered into an 
agreement that requires PJM to run the energy markets and to submit filings under section 205, 
PJM can only submit those filings on behalf of the Members, not on its own behalf. 
The allocation of section 205 filing rights falls squarely within “contract rates” afforded 
Mobile-Sierra protection.23  As Atlantic City Electric Company states, public utilities may only 
cede their section 205 filing rights “voluntarily,” that is “by contract” under the Mobile-Sierra 
 
19 United Gas Pipe Line Co. v. Mobile Gas Serv. Corp., 350 U.S. 332 (1956); FPC v. Sierra Pac. Power Co., 350 
U.S. 348 (1956). 
20 Morgan Stanley Cap. Grp. Inc. v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1, 554 U.S. 527, 534, 551 (2008) (quoting Permian Basin 
Area Rate Cases, 390 U.S. 747, 822 (1968)). 
21 Operating Agreement, Section 8.8(ii). 
22 Operating Agreement, Section 10.4(xiii). 
23 NRG Power Mktg., LLC v. Me. PUC, 558 U.S. 165, 176 (2010).

10 
 
doctrine,24 and the Commission has approved Mobile-Sierra’s application to such allocations of 
filing rights between transmission owners and independent system operators across markets.25  
In addition, Sections 8.8 and 10.4 are the product of arm’s-length negotiations rather than 
negotiations “aimed at protecting a common interest” among competitors.26  Sophisticated parties 
freely negotiated these terms nearly thirty years ago in order to put in place an Independent System 
Operator for the PJM Power Pool.  From January through May 1997, transmission owners and a 
“large group of interested stakeholders”—including “two major independent power producers” 
and “two major power marketers”—“met continuously” with “the assistance of a professional 
facilitator” to “resolve or narrow differences” and “forge consensus where possible” on issues of 
“ISO governance, reliability, transmission service and the structure of the energy market.”27  The 
powers of the Members Committee were among those provisions where “compromise” was 
achieved.28  The Supporting Companies Filing of the PJM Governing Documents stated that the 
“proposal to utilize sector voting” for the Members Committee “is the product of compromise with 
other stakeholders, even though it is not [their] preferred approach.”29   
 
24 Atl. City Elec. Co. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 11 (D.C. Cir. 2002). 
25 See Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland Interconnection, 105 FERC ¶ 61,294, at PP 32-33 (2003); PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., 108 FERC ¶ 61,318, at P 66 (2004) (finding that Mobile-Sierra application to the allocation 
of all filing rights between PJM and PJM Transmission Owners applies to “all transmission owner filings”); ISO 
New England Inc., 106 FERC ¶ 61,280, at P 127 (2004) (approving application of Mobile-Sierra to allocation of 
filing rights to transmission owners); Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 110 FERC ¶ 61,380, at 
PP 19, 25-26 (2005) (approving application of Mobile-Sierra to allocation of filing rights). 
26 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 142 FERC ¶ 61,214, at P 189 (2013). 
27 Filing of the PJM Supporting Companies, Docket Nos. ER97-3189-000, et al., Transmittal at 1-2, 6 (June 2, 1997) 
(Filing of PJM Governing Documents). 
28 Id., Transmittal at 6. 
29 Id., Attachment B at 3 n.1 (Compliance with Criteria for an Independent System Operator); see Pennsylvania-New 
Jersey-Maryland Interconnection, 81 FERC ¶ 61,257, at 62,261-70 (1997) (conditionally accepting the Supporting 
Companies proposal to restructure PJM as an ISO and form the PJM Operating Agreement, Transmission Owners 
Agreement, Tariff, and Reliability Assurance Agreement), reh’g denied, 92 FERC ¶ 61,282 (2000), modified sub 
nom. Atl. City Elec. Co., 295 F.3d 1.

11 
 
Moreover, while Sections 8.8 and 10.4 apply to all Members, they preserve the existing rights 
of public utilities and do not “delimit, qualify, or restrict”30 the ability of any other market 
participant.  The “division of responsibility” between PJM and its Members “affect[s], 
predominantly[,] the contracting parties alone.”31  New Members have the same rights as the 
original parties.  Non-market generators and transmission owners retain their individual section 
205 filing rights, and all parties retain section 205 filing rights via the Members Committee, where 
“each major segment of the industry is assured a say” and “no one sector can force the Members 
Committee to act, and no one sector can block the Members Committee from acting.”32  Indeed, 
the Commission previously found that similar allocation of filing rights “adequately safeguarded 
the interests of the region as a whole.”33 
Relatedly, some argue that governance structures in other RTOs/ISOs that permit the RTO/ISO 
to file energy and ancillary services market rule changes under section 205 should apply in PJM.34  
But even if other RTOs/ISOs may have section 205 authority that PJM does not, that precedent is 
not binding on PJM.  “The Commission has long recognized regional differences in each of the 
RTOs/ISOs and has specifically allowed for regional differences in RTOs’ governance structure.”35  
These differences make sense given “other RTOs/ISOs have different governance structures that 
 
30 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 142 FERC ¶ 61,214, at P 186. 
31 ISO New England Inc., 106 FERC ¶ 61,280, at P 130. 
32 PJM Governing Documents, Attachment B at 3. 
33 Midwest Indep. Transmission Sys. Operator, Inc., 110 FERC ¶ 61,380, at P 19. 
34 See, e.g., PJM Pre-Conference Comments at 8; Commission-Led Technical Conference on PJM Governance and 
Stakeholder Reforms, Docket No. AD26-7-000, at 2:25:21 - 2:27:36 (July 23, 2026), https://www.ferc.gov/news-
events/events/PJM-Governance-Stakeholder-Reforms (Tech. Conf. Video) (PJM President and CEO, David Mills, 
discussing section 205 rights over the energy and ancillary services markets). 
35 Duquesne Light Co., 189 FERC ¶ 61,181, at P 108 (citing Order Nos. 1000 and 2000); see, e.g., Midcontinent 
Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 162 FERC ¶ 61,176, at P 57 (2018) (“[T]he Commission has consistently rejected a one-
size-fits-all approach in the various RTOs/ISOs due, in large part, to significant differences between each region and 
that there can be more than one just and reasonable rate.”).

12 
 
were arrived at through negotiations and tradeoffs that balance the rights and obligations of diverse 
stakeholders.”36  The division of filing rights in PJM reflect the stakeholder tradeoffs that were 
negotiated in PJM to balance the rights and obligations among PJM stakeholders and the 
agreements struck among stakeholders in other regions does not reflect the PJM balance. 
Investor Concerns Are Likely to Rise if PJM Authority Is Increased 
The Commission should refrain from fundamentally overhauling filing rights in PJM, 
especially at this critical time when significant investment is needed to meet tightening system 
conditions; simply put, a governance overhaul that includes additional PJM filing rights could 
undermine investor confidence in PJM at a time when their investment is most needed.  Investor 
confidence and willingness to invest in assets in PJM is shaped by (among other things) PJM 
market outcomes and expectations in the rules that shape those market outcomes into the future.  
Actions by PJM that are counter to competitive market results undermine investor confidence in 
the markets and the desire by competitors (and their owners) to invest.  The bottom line is that 
PJM has failed to appropriately consider investor impact in exercising the section 205 authority 
over resource adequacy matters it already has.  This is inconsistent with the Commission’s and 
Administration’s desire to instill investor confidence and incent new infrastructure in PJM.37  And, 
against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to justify increasing PJM’s filing authority. 
 
36 Duquesne Light Co., 189 FERC ¶ 61,181, at P 108. 
37 Chairman Laura Swett, Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD, FERC 
(May 12, 2026), https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-meeting-
baltimore-md-0 (“[W]e cannot disrupt finalized commercial agreements.  At FERC, I have no appetite to 
compromise investor confidence when those investors are driving the buildout of the generation that PJM 
desperately needs.”); Tech. Conf. Video at 45:30-46:50 (the Honorable James P. Danly discussing the need to right 
the capacity market with immediate resolution: “We are facing demand signals like we’ve never seen before. . . .  
Don’t lose sight of the fact that we actually have to fix the problems that are inhibiting the biggest problem we have 
which is getting as much supply online as quickly as possible and doing so while protecting ratepayers. . . .  PJM’s 
Board and as an institution needs to recommit itself to the market functions it was originally designed to oversee and 
execute.”), 55:40-55:52 (Peter Lake: “[I]f were gonna have a market we’ve got to let it work.”), 56:55-57:27 (Peter 
Lake: “[T]his is the only industry in the world that can stare in the face of trillions of dollars of expected investment 
and argue amongst each other so effectively as to scare off that investment.”).

13 
 
For example, in February 2025, PJM filed—without Member Committee authorization—a 
collar mechanism to apply in the capacity market during delivery years 2026/27 and 2027/28.  PJM 
made this filing pursuant to existing authority to file under section 205 with respect to resource 
adequacy matters.38  A little over a year later, PJM filed to extend the collar to also cover the 
2028/29 and 2029/30 delivery years, again filing under section 205, based on its existing authority 
and without Member Committee authorization.39  The signal to investors from these repeated 
exercises of PJM’s section 205 filing rights is that market supply/demand fundamentals cannot be 
counted on in PJM to support new investment; in other words, investors have learned to expect 
PJM to curb actual market results whenever supply becomes tight compared to demand in PJM,40 
and they must factor that PJM intervention expectation when deciding whether to invest through 
market mechanisms.  As a result, in part, of PJM’s repeated artificial reductions in capacity market 
prices, investors will hesitate to bring new investment through the capacity market.  Indeed only 
524.7 MWs of new resources entered in PJM’s most recent capacity market auction, although some 
of the reticence was undoubtedly caused by the knowledge that the Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (RBP) was around the corner.41  Instead, investors will require something more (e.g., 
a long-term, out-of-market contract such as those available under the RBP) before they will invest 
in the region, and this out-of-market contracting will be more costly in the long run compared to 
 
38 Proposal for Revised Price Cap and Price Floor for the 2026/2027 and 2027/2028 Delivery Years of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER25-1357, at 6 (Feb. 20, 2025) (Initial Collar Filing).  
39 Proposal to Extend the Price Cap and Price Floor for the 2028/2029 and 2029/2030 Delivery Years of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-1556, at 6 (Feb. 27, 2026) (Collar Extension). 
40 Recent price trends in the oil industry provide a simple example of how supply/demand fundamentals would 
typically affect price-outcome expectations.  World oil market prices have increased, as restrictions on oil shipments 
(i.e., supply) through the Strait of Hormuz and uncertainty related to such shipments has increased.  Conversely, oil 
prices have decreased as shipment certainty has increased.   
41 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction Report, PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 3, 7-8 (July 14, 2026), 
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2028-2029/2028-2029-bra-results-
report.pdf.

14 
 
the market-driven approach.   Given PJM’s repeated interventions in market outcomes, in order for 
PJM to restore market integrity and investor confidence, it will have to intentionally and 
consistently embrace competitive markets that reflect market fundamentals.  With the current RBP 
proposal, Constellation is concerned that more of the inefficient out-of-market intervention likely 
will be required. 
PJM has filed numerous other changes recently to resource adequacy market rules under its 
existing section 205 authority that similarly undermine market outcomes and investor confidence 
including: the DPL-South market rerun;42 the treatment of Brandon Shores and Wagner as price 
takers in capacity auctions despite not providing a Capacity Performance product;43 and PJM’s 
proposal to treat RBP resources as price takers.44   
During the technical conference, PJM’s Senior Director of Stakeholder Affairs, David Anders, 
explained that when PJM was initially formed, the asset owners did not have confidence in PJM, 
so they intentionally kept the transmission planning and energy and ancillary services markets 
matters in the Operating Agreement so Members could retain oversight.45  Given PJM’s extensive 
market-undermining use of the section 205 authority it already has, Constellation, a significant 
asset owner in PJM, has little confidence in how PJM has used its existing section 205 authority 
 
42 See PJM Power Providers Grp. v. FERC, 96 F.4th 390 (3d Cir. 2024). 
43 See H.A. Wagner LLC, 187 FERC ¶ 61,176 (2024), order on contested settlement, 191 FERC ¶ 61,098, order on 
reh’g, 192 FERC ¶ 61,189 (2025), appeal pending, Petition for Review, Maryland Office of People’s Counsel v. 
FERC, No. 26-1050 (D.C. Cir. Mar. 2, 2026). 
44 See Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns Stemming from Large Loads of 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3380-000, at 56-60, 129-30 (July 31, 2026); Limited Protest of

12. Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over the energy market and ancillary 
services unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds of the 
Members Committee? 
No.  See our response to Question 11.  
13. Should PJM have section 205 filing rights over Regional Transmission Expansion 
Planning (RTEP) unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds of 
the Members Committee? 
No.  See our response to Question 11.  However, Constellation acknowledges that extending 
section 205 filing rights to PJM for non-market matters raises issues that are different than filing 
rights over market matters. 
14. Should the Organization of PJM States Inc (OPSI) have “jump ball” rights over 
resource adequacy and transmission cost allocation filings when a supermajority of 
OPSI agrees on an alternative proposal? 
No.  States and organizations representing state interests seeking changes to PJM’s Tariff, 
market rules, or other governing documents have long-established rights to pursue such changes 
under the FPA,46 and state entities have proven well-capable of exercising these rights.47  However, 
it would be inconsistent with the FPA for the states to have such rights, jump ball or otherwise.48  
In addition, as elaborated above in response to Question 11, even if some RTO/ISO allows a jump 
ball right for certain membership organizations, those RTO/ISO rules are not dispositive for PJM.

No.  Constellation supports retention of existing rights rather than the addition of “jump ball”

B. Stakeholder Process 
16. Should the approval threshold in the Members Committee be lowered from two-thirds 
sector-weighted voting? 
Yes.  If the PJM Members Committee agrees to such a change, reducing the voting threshold 
to a majority vote could support the Commission’s goal of facilitating section 205 filings without 
upending PJM’s existing governance structure as some have suggested.   
17. Should the voting rules barring affiliate votes, which apply to senior standing 
committees, also apply to lower-level committees? 
 
No.  Affiliate voting is an important component for balancing interests within the PJM voting 
structure.  Discussion at the lower level committees—where affiliate voting is relied on—are 
usually more technical and detailed in nature and having the diversity of interests makes for a more 
robust vetting of issues.  At the senior level committees (Markets and Reliability and Members 
Committees) each Member has only one vote, consolidating the interests to the primary voting 
member on matters that have already been largely shaped at the lower committee. 
C. State Participation 
18. In addition to OPSI, should there be a second state representative group consisting of 
governors’ representatives and/or state legislators’ representatives? 
Yes.  However, Constellation sees two potential approaches for enhancing governor 
representation: (1) the “right-sizing” of OPSI, including increased staffing levels so it can cover

17 
 
its existing constituents as well as an OPSI-enhanced role in representing governors’ and 
legislators’ interests; or (2) creating and funding a separate entity representing PJM governors and 
legislators.    
In addition to providing these additional resources, protocols should be established for PJM to 
meet regularly with state commissioners and/or commission staff to seek input on important 
market and transmission issues, rule changes, and other concerns, including both staff-to-staff and 
leadership-to-leadership meetings.  Also, clear processes for state commissions to request and 
receive technical information and support on matters related to wholesale markets and/or 
infrastructure planning and their interactions with state regulation and retail rates should be 
established. 
19. Should state representatives have a formal voting role in the stakeholder process 
(limited to certain topics, such as resource adequacy and regional transmission cost 
allocation) in addition to the consumer advocate votes?   
No.  Consumer interests are already represented through the state-designated consumer 
advocates.  The relationship between state commissions and PJM was developed in a 2005 
Memorandum of Understanding between PJM and OPSI which stated that while commissioners 
and their staff participate, deliberate, give input, and engage at all levels of the PJM stakeholder 
process they do not vote on any issue.49  Since then, state commissions and representatives have 
participated in the stakeholder process and have done so very effectively.  For example, the current 
Variable Resource Requirement curve that was endorsed by Members and approved by the 
Commission was based on a joint proposal between PJM and the office of the Vice Chair of the

Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission,50 and at OPSI’s request, PJM facilitated the Clean

States are sovereign regulators and policy makers with the ability to make policy decisions that 
are outside of PJM jurisdiction.  That said, states can and have played an important, non-voting, 
role in the PJM stakeholder process; including, for example, the initiation of the Sub-Annual

interact with PJM staff and the PJM Board that are not available to voting Members, some of which 
are discussed in the 2005 Memorandum of Understanding.  To the extent that those opportunities 
need to be enhanced or expanded, such as assigning a PJM Board member to act as a liaison with 
each state, Constellation welcomes further discussion on this matter.  However, providing the states 
with an additional voting role at PJM would elevate their status compared to existing PJM voting 
Members, including the state consumer advocates who have a critical role in representing retail 
ratepayers.  Amending the Operating Agreement to include state commissions or representatives 
undermines that current, balanced governing structure at PJM that ensures that no Member has 
undue influence while recognizing and supporting the state’s important, non-voting role in the PJM 
stakeholder process and community.
